# Rex plans

A Rex plan is one unit of work (a feature, a fix, a migration) saved as JSON at `rex/plans/<name>.rex.json` in the repo, committed with the code. Rex attaches to the plan file you write and shows it live as an outline next to the agent tape, with the task you are on pinned. You write the plan, its statuses and its completion fields; Rex only reads the file. Rex has no actions of its own: never tell the person to create, open, pin or mark anything done in Rex. Rex never sends you anything either; the plan file is how a new chat picks up the work.

The format is frozen at `"version": 1`; the full contract is `docs/plan-format.md` in the Rex repo.

## When to plan

- You are asked to plan, to break work down, or to fill or refine a `.rex.json`.
- The work is bigger than one PR. One plan per unit of work; a second feature gets its own file.
- Do not create a plan for a one-line fix, and do not add tasks for work nobody asked for.

## Writing the file

- Write it yourself at `rex/plans/<name>.rex.json` under the repo root (`rex/plans/<area>/<name>.rex.json` groups plans), creating the folders if they are missing. `<name>` is a short slug, usually the plan's `id`.
- Use your file write or edit tool, not a shell redirect or a script: Rex follows the file edits your hooks report, and a shell command that writes the file is not one of them.
- Write valid JSON each time you save. Writing the whole plan at once works, and so does a first save with an empty `tasks` array that you fill next; the outline updates as the file changes.
- To fill or refine a plan that exists, edit that file in place and keep every other byte.
- A running Rex that is following opens it; if the person picked another plan, Rex offers yours on its status line. Don't ask them to create or open it in Rex.

## The shape

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "id": "card-highlight",
  "title": "Selected plan card is one block",
  "goal": "One paragraph: what this work is for and what will be true when it is done.",
  "status": "pending",
  "base": "main",
  "scope": {
    "in": ["the hard edges of the job"],
    "out": ["what this work must not touch"]
  },
  "tasks": [
    {
      "id": "card-bar",
      "title": "Bar spans the whole card",
      "parent": "",
      "status": "pending",
      "needs": ["what must already be true before starting"],
      "does": ["what will be true when this task is done"],
      "description": "longer intent, only if title and does are not enough",
      "depends_on": [],
      "verify": ["go test ./internal/tui -run PlanCard", "Open latest: ▌ on all three card rows"],
      "files": ["internal/tui/plans.go"],
      "branch": "feature/card_bar",
      "scope": {"in": [], "out": []},
      "accomplished": [],
      "modified": [],
      "verified_how": [],
      "completed_notes": ""
    }
  ]
}
```

Plan fields: `version`, `id`, `title`, `goal`, `status`, `base`, `scope` (`in`, `out`), `tasks`.
Task fields: `id`, `title`, `parent`, `status`, `scope`, `needs`, `does`, `description`, `depends_on`, `verify`, `files`, `branch`, and the completion fields `accomplished`, `modified`, `verified_how`, `completed_notes`.

## Rules

- **ids** are short, stable slugs (`card-bar`). Never renumber or reuse them; other tasks and PRs refer to them.
- **The tasks array is flat**, in the order the work should be done, which is also the order its PRs stack. Do not nest `children`.
- **`parent`** is outline: the task sits under that heading. **`depends_on`** is order: hard prerequisites only, the tasks that must be `done` (or `skipped`) first, always earlier in the file. They are independent; a task can sit under "UI" and depend on a task under "storage".
- Only leaf tasks (nobody's parent) get pinned. Keep the outline two or three levels deep; deeper means a second plan.
- **One task, one PR** a human can review in one sitting. If it is bigger, split it.
- **`needs` vs `does`.** `needs` is what must already be true ("the pick colors exist"); `does` is what will be true when the task is done ("the bar spans all three rows"). Keep them apart; merged, nobody can tell "we still lack X" from "we will ship X".
- **`verify`** is how a stranger would check it: commands or observations. **`files`** are the paths or globs the task will edit. They are not a lock, but Rex reads them: an edit outside every folder the pinned task lists shows as drift, so list each folder the task really touches.
- **`scope.out`** is the hard edge: what this work must not touch. Rex matches its entries against prompts and edited paths, so write short nouns or path words ("extra palettes", "web UI", "internal/jsonedit/**"), not sentences ("do not change the public API of …").
- **`status`** is one of `pending`, `active`, `done`, `blocked`, `skipped`. At most one leaf task (one that is nobody's `parent`) is `active`: that is the pin, the task being worked. A parent marked `active` is only a label. Write status down; do not leave it to be inferred.

## Stacked PRs

Rex never runs git or opens a PR. A plan can still be shaped so each task lands as one PR in a stack, and whoever works a task works out from the plan where its PR goes.

- **Opt in with `base`**: the branch the stack lands on, the trunk this repo starts work from (its AGENTS.md or CONTRIBUTING says; else `git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` minus `origin/`). A plan that builds on another unmerged stack names that stack's top branch.
- **One leaf task, one PR.** Parents are headings, never PRs, and get no `branch`. `skipped` tasks have no PR.
- **The stack is file order.** The first leaf's PR targets `base`; each next leaf's targets the branch of the leaf before it. Each task builds and passes its tests on the tasks before it alone, and `depends_on` names only earlier tasks; Rex reports one that points later.
- **One plan, one stack.** Tasks that need none of each other's code still stack, in the order they should land. Work that must merge on its own goes in its own plan.
- **`branch`**: name every leaf's branch up front, the way this repo names branches (`feature/card_bar` here). Plain names only: letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-`, `/`, at most 80 bytes; Rex reports any other name. One per task, never the same as `base`.
- **Changing a stack.** Reorder freely before work starts. Once branches exist, add new work as a new task at the end rather than moving one, and fix a lower PR with a commit on its branch.

## Never in a plan

- prompts, system prompts or nudges for an agent;
- auto-approve lists or tool permissions;
- diffs or file bodies;
- secrets;
- timestamps that change on every save.

## Working a plan

When you are asked to work, continue or pick up a plan, or a task of one, the plan file is the hand-off: read it first, and **re-read it at the start of every turn** while you work it, since the person or another agent may have changed it.

- **Which plan.** The one the person names. If they name none: the plan you wrote or worked in this conversation; else the plan under `rex/plans/` whose top-level `status` is `active` (the most recently modified, if several are); else ask.
- **The current task** is the leaf task with `"status": "active"`. If none is, it is the first `pending` leaf, in file order, whose `depends_on` are all `done` or `skipped`. If the person names a task, that one. Work only on it, stay inside its scope and out of the plan's `scope.out`, and if the plan is wrong, edit the JSON rather than working around it.
- **Starting a task.** Set that leaf's `status` to `active`, set any other `active` leaf to `pending`, and set the plan's own `status` to `active` if it was `pending` or `done`. Never write a parent's status. Rex shows the change at once: that is how the person sees what you are on.
- **Finishing a task.** Once its work is done and checked (and, in a stack, its PR is open), fill its completion fields:
  - `accomplished`: what actually happened (a retrospective, not a copy of `does`);
  - `modified`: the paths you actually changed;
  - `verified_how`: how you actually checked it;
  - `completed_notes`: anything the next chat should know.

  Then set its `status` to `done`, in the same save if you can. Leave `branch` as it is: the next task finds the PR below by it. If every leaf task is now `done` or `skipped`, then set the plan's own top-level `status` to `done`; parent tasks don't need a status of their own. Then stop and report. Start the next task only when the person asks: each task is one PR.
- **Editing the file.** Edit only the members you change, inside the task objects you change (plus the plan's own `status`), keep every other byte as it is, never reformat the file, and never mark a task done that you did not finish.

### Review before the PR

Before you open the task's PR, mark it ready, or push new commits to it, review it read-only. If the repo has its own review rules, follow those instead.

- **Reviewers change nothing.** Each one reads the diff and the code, runs what it needs in a scratch copy outside the repo, and reports each finding with a severity (blocker: must not merge; major: wrong or risky, fix it before the PR or explain why not; minor: worth fixing now; nit: polish), file:line, evidence and a suggested fix. If you can start subagents, give each job its own read-only subagent, side by side; otherwise do the passes yourself, one at a time, without editing in between.
- **One job each:**
  - **Design:** how the change fits the system: effects across modules, failure modes, the repo's rules and the task's scope.
  - **UI**, only when the UI or CLI output changed: drive it like a user, in an isolated session, at narrow and wide sizes.
  - **Break it:** hostile inputs, edge cases, concurrency, and regressions against the base branch, with tests that fail before a fix.
  - **Lint:** the repo's formatter, linters, type checks and pre-PR gate, and docs the change made stale.
- **Then fix** each finding, with a test where it can have one, or say in the PR body why you skipped it. The reviewers' runs are theirs: `verified_how` names the check you ran yourself.
- **Then a final readiness check:** one more read-only pass over the fixed branch: the diff, the tests and their output, the PR body (problem, what changed, why, how, tests run, captures for UI changes) and the issue it closes. Repeat while it still finds blockers or majors that are neither fixed nor explained, then open or update the PR.

### Its PR, when the plan is a stack

A plan is a stack when it names a `base` or a task names a `branch`. Work out where the current task's PR goes from the plan alone:

- **Branch:** the task's `branch`. If it has none, name one the way this repo names branches.
- **Base:** the `branch` of the nearest earlier leaf task that is `done`; with none, the plan's `base` (without one, the repo's trunk). Skipped tasks don't count. Once that PR has merged, the base is the plan's `base`.
- **Below it, not done yet:** earlier leaves that are not `done` or `skipped`. Each joins the stack under this PR when it is done.
- **Above it, already done:** later leaves that are `done`. Their PRs sit on this one and move when it changes.

Do these steps when the repo's own rules for a PR are met (its checks, the review above, and its PR body):

1. **Cut.** Create the branch from the base (`git switch -c <branch> <base>`). If it already exists (an earlier chat started it, or the task was reopened), switch to it and add commits rather than amending them. If it isn't on the base yet (the base moved, or a lower task finished since), rebase it onto the base with `--autostash` and retarget its PR. If the PR below has merged, cut from the plan's `base`; after a squash merge, move an existing branch with `git rebase --autostash --onto <plan base> <old base> <branch>`. If the PR below was closed without merging, stop and ask.
2. **Record.** If the plan has no branch for this task, or you used another name, write it as this task's `"branch"`, touching nothing else.
3. **Keep one plan.** Rex reads the plan file from the working tree, and it is the stack's, not one PR's:
   - Commit it only where every stack branch will hold it: on the trunk before the first branch is cut (if that goes through a PR, wait for it to merge and pull the trunk first), or once the stack has landed. While the stack is in flight, never stage or commit it on any branch, a stack branch or one of its own: `git add` only your task's files, not `-A` or `commit -a`. Then every branch holds the same copy (or none), and its changes in the working tree follow you across `git switch` and `git rebase --autostash`. Its progress stays in the checkout Rex runs in until the stack lands, so work the stack from there.
   - If a rebase stops on a conflict, `git add` only the files you resolved, never the plan, and finish it before you edit the plan again.
   - Check that no stack branch committed it: `git log --oneline <trunk>..<top branch> -- <plan>` prints nothing. If one did, copy the plan out of the repo, then on that branch make a new commit that puts back the trunk's copy (`git restore --source <trunk> --staged --worktree -- <plan>`; when the trunk has none, `git rm --cached <plan>` and then remove the working copy, which you have outside), restack, and copy the plan back.
4. **Open.** Push and open the PR against the base, not the trunk. In the body, name the plan file and the task's id, the PR it sits on, and that the stack merges bottom-up. On GitHub: `gh pr create --base <base> --head <branch>`.
5. **Link.** On GitHub with the `github/gh-stack` extension: `gh stack link --base <plan base> <every branch of the stack, bottom to top, yours in its place>`. `--base` is the base of the first branch listed, and link corrects the PR bases it is given, so never start the list in the middle. Leave out branches whose PR merged. Without the extension, or on GitLab, Gitea or Bitbucket, the chain of base branches is the stack: open each PR or MR against the one below, and merge bottom-up. Don't install extensions unless asked.
6. **Restack.** If later leaves are already done, your commits moved what their PRs sit on. After pushing, check out the top branch and run `git rebase --autostash --update-refs <your branch>` (Git 2.38+; it moves every branch in between, and `--autostash` keeps the plan's changes), then `git push --force-with-lease` each moved branch, and check that the PR just above targets your branch. Leave out any whose PR merged.
